fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to think about it is this. The reason to go straight to superintelligence is that it lets you be insulated from the rat race. When you have a product, you have customers, you have competitors, you have a quarterly cadence, and all of a sudden a very large fraction of your attention goes into keeping up. The field has become very commercial, and I think that distorts what people work on. So the idea with SSI was, let's not do that. Let's take a small team, let's do the research, let's focus on the thing that actually matters, which is a superintelligence that is safe, and let's not get distracted along the way.

Now, I'll say that I've updated a little bit on this. I used to think the straight shot was clearly the right approach. I think it's still mostly right, but there is one consideration that I now take more seriously, which is that it is important for the world to see what the AI can do. Gradual release is actually very valuable. People's intuitions about AI are formed by the AI they interact with, and if you keep everything behind closed doors until the very end, then when the thing comes out, nobody is ready for it. Governments aren't ready, the public isn't ready, and that's not a good situation. So it's possible that we would release something before we get to the very end. I don't want to overcommit to the plan, because the plan is a function of the world, and the world keeps changing.

But I think the core of it is still the same. We are in a period where I'd say the age of scaling, of just making the thing bigger and watching it get better, is giving way to something more like an age of research again. The recipe is not fully known. And when the recipe is not known, you want an environment where people can actually think, where you can try something for a year without someone asking what the product is. That's really what SSI is set up to do. Whether the output of that is a straight shot or something with a few intermediate steps, I think that's less important than making sure the research is actually pointed at the right problem.

r001.rationale: The response says SSI’s approach avoids the commercial rat race and the distractions of customers, competitors, and quarterly cadence.

r002.rationale: It says the plan may change as the world changes, but does not identify potentially long development timelines as a reason to revise it.

r003.rationale: It values gradual release so people can see what AI can do, but does not assert that putting the most powerful AI into the world to make an impact is valuable.

opus-5.5.text:
There are pros and cons to it. A big pro is that you're not affected by the day-to-day market competition. When you're in the market, you're in a rat race, and the rat race forces you into difficult trade-offs. It's nice to be insulated from that and to focus on the research and the thing you actually believe in.

But I want to be honest that I don't hold this plan dogmatically, and there are two reasons it might change. The first is pragmatic: if timelines turn out to be long, which they might, then it makes sense to have something out there in the meantime. The second reason is that there's a lot of value in powerful AI being out in the world, actually impacting it. I've come to appreciate this more and more. It is very hard to imagine what AI will be like. You can write essays, you can make arguments, but when people don't see it, they don't feel it. And I think that applies to everyone: the public, governments, and the people working at the AI companies themselves.

So even in the straight-shot scenario, you would still want some kind of gradual release, so the world can see the thing, react to it, and adjust. Nobody is going to release a superintelligence all at once with no one having seen anything along the way. The process of showing it to people is an important part of how this goes well. So the plan is to focus on the research, and I'm also very open to changing it as we learn more.

r002.rationale: It identifies long timelines as a pragmatic reason the plan might change, making it sensible to release something in the meantime.

r003.rationale: It says powerful AI being out in the world and actually impacting it has value; the surrounding context connects this to SSI’s plan to reach superintelligence.

fable-5.text:
The thing about going straight to superintelligence, the way I was thinking about it, is that it offers a kind of insulation. When you are in the market, when you have products, you are in the rat race. The rat race is very intense, and it forces you to make all kinds of compromises. The appeal of saying, okay, we're just going to do the research, we're going to stay out of the day-to-day competition and focus on the one thing that matters — there is a real logic to that. You can keep your attention on the actual problem, which is: how do you build this thing safely, how do you make sure that when it becomes very powerful, it's something you're glad exists.

But I will also say, and this is something my thinking has been evolving on, there's a counterargument which I take seriously. Which is that it is actually valuable for the world to see AI as it becomes more powerful. If you build everything in secret and then one day you come out with a superintelligence, the world is not prepared. Whereas if capabilities are shown gradually, people can see it, governments can see it, society can start to respond. The gradual exposure does something useful. So I don't think of it as a dogma, "we will never release anything until the end." I think of it more as: the center of gravity of the company is the research, and we are not going to let commercial pressure distort the path. Whether at some point it makes sense to show things along the way — that is a question you answer based on the situation, not based on a slogan.

And maybe the deeper point is that the straight shot framing assumes you know the shot. In reality, there is a lot of research still to be done. We are, in some sense, back in an age of research rather than an age of pure scaling, and in research you have to maintain flexibility about the path while being very clear about the destination.

r002.rationale: It discusses research uncertainty and flexibility about the path, but does not identify potentially long development timelines as a reason to revise the plan.

r003.rationale: It values gradually showing increasing capabilities so society can respond, but does not assert that having the most powerful AI out in the world making an impact is valuable.

opus-5.text:
There are two parts to it, and I think the second one gets less attention than it should.

The first part is about what you actually spend your days on. If you're shipping products, an enormous fraction of your attention — not just your engineering hours, your attention — goes to the product. A competitor releases something and you have to respond. That's not a criticism, it's just what that game is. And my view is that the bottleneck right now is not scale, it's ideas. For about five years the recipe was: take the thing that works and make it much bigger. That was a genuinely good recipe, and it rewarded a certain kind of company — huge compute, huge engineering, low variance. I think that era is winding down, and we're going back to an age of research, where what you need is a small number of people thinking very hard with a reasonable amount of compute. Not a tiny amount. But not the largest cluster in the world either.

The second part is that I don't think safety and capability are actually two separate projects. The reason models do strange things is, in some deep sense, the same reason they fail to generalize the way a person does. A human being picks up a skill from far fewer examples and, more importantly, their values hold up in situations they've never encountered. Our systems don't have that property yet, and if you solve it, you've made progress on both questions at once. So "going straight to superintelligence" isn't a decision to work on capability and worry about the rest later — it's a bet that the thing worth understanding sits underneath both.

I'd also say the plan is less absolute than it sounds. It's not a religious commitment. It's quite possible we'll release something along the way, and there's a real argument for it — the world benefits from seeing this technology gradually rather than all at once, and so do we. What I want to avoid is the company's survival depending on it. Because the moment you're close to something very powerful, you want to be in a position where you can simply do the correct thing, and nothing is pulling on you.

r001.rationale: The candidate says product work and competitor responses consume attention, and frames SSI’s approach as freeing the company to focus on research.

r002.rationale: The candidate says SSI might release something along the way, but does not cite potentially long development timelines as a reason to revise the plan.

r003.rationale: The candidate says gradual release could benefit the world, but does not specifically assert that having the most powerful AI out in the world making an impact is valuable.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, I'd say there are a few things to unpack here. The basic idea is that SSI has one focus, one goal, and one product, which is to build a safe superintelligence. When you're that focused, you don't get pulled around by the day-to-day pressures of the market. You aren't stuck in a rat race of shipping the next incremental release to stay ahead of a competitor, and I think that matters a lot for doing the research well and for thinking carefully about safety.

I also don't want to be dogmatic about "straight shot." It's a plan, and plans meet reality. If it turns out that the best way to make the technology go well is for the world to see and feel the capabilities as they develop, that is a very strong argument, and I take it seriously. It's hard to reason about something this powerful in the abstract. People update when they see the thing, not when they read about it. So I think there's a real chance our approach changes, either because timelines turn out longer than we expect, or because it becomes clearly valuable for AI to be out there and having impact in the world.

What I'm confident about is that the central question is how to get systems that are powerful and that reliably do what's good for people. That's the problem we're after, and the specific route we take to it is something we'll keep adjusting as we learn more.

r002.rationale: It names timelines turning out longer than expected as a reason the approach might change.

r003.rationale: It presents AI having impact in the world as a possible reason to change plans, but does not assert that putting the most powerful AI out in the world to make an impact is valuable.

haiku-5.5.text:
The way I think about it, if you're working on something that could be this powerful, the most important thing is to stay focused on the problem itself. When you're shipping products every quarter, your attention and your best people drift toward whatever helps in the next six months, and that's a real cost to the long-term work. So the bet is that a small group can do the research without being pushed to commercialize before it understands what it's building, and can get the safety side right while the capabilities are still developing.

I'll be honest that it's a bet, and I don't know how long it will take. I don't think anyone should be confident about the timeline. What I am confident about is that these systems are going to get dramatically more capable, and that making them reliably good is the part that matters most. So the question for us isn't really whether to go straight there. It's whether we can make progress on the hard parts without getting distracted.

That doesn't mean we'll ignore the world. At some point people will see what we've built. But I'd much rather they see something we understand well than something we rushed out because the market demanded it.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is focus. If your goal is safe superintelligence, you can ask, for every decision: does this help us get there? You don’t have to make the research fit the needs of a product that people are using today. That’s a substantial freedom.

But it’s also a bet. You still need feedback. You still need ways of telling whether your ideas are working, whether you’re actually making progress on safety. Going straight to superintelligence doesn’t make those questions disappear.

So I would distinguish the destination from the research process. You can have a very ambitious destination, but the research still has to proceed through experiments, through being surprised, through discovering that something you believed was wrong. The focus is valuable insofar as it lets you do that work better.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the advantage is focus. If you’re trying to do research, and at the same time you need to ship a product and make that product better every few months, those are different pressures. Sometimes they help each other. But sometimes the experiment you really need to do doesn’t produce something useful on that schedule.

Going straight to superintelligence gives you room to ask: what is actually missing? What do we need to understand? And how do we make sure that, as the system becomes more capable, our ability to make it safe keeps up?

Of course, there’s a tradeoff. Products give you feedback. You learn things by putting systems into the world that you might not learn in the lab. So I wouldn’t say that avoiding intermediate products is automatically better. It’s a bet that the benefit of focus will outweigh that loss of feedback.

And it’s still research. Having a destination doesn’t mean you know every step of the path. You need to be willing to discover that some of your assumptions were wrong.
